text: ping, traceroute, and dig confirm a host is reachable and that DNS resolves correctly. This lesson moves one layer up: once a host responds, is the actual application answering correctly, and what's actually listening on that machine locally? It's also where one of the most common failure patterns shows up: a server that pings just fine but won't actually serve the page.

An HTTP response's status code is the first signal worth reading. Two hundred means the request succeeded. Four-oh-four means the specific path doesn't exist on an otherwise working server. Five hundred means the server received the request but hit an internal error handling it. And a connection that's refused or times out means the problem never even reached the application — that's still network or firewall territory.

curl makes the actual HTTP request and shows the real response — status code, headers, and body — with none of a browser's rendering or caching in the way. Here, a two-hundred and a clean JSON body confirm the health endpoint itself is working correctly, nginx and all.

ss answers a related question from inside the machine itself: which ports is this server actually listening on right now. Running it here confirms the application process is actually bound to the port it's supposed to be, which is a precondition no amount of firewall tuning can substitute for.

A server that pings fine but refuses every connection to its actual application port is one of the most common failure shapes out there — and ss on the server itself usually settles the question immediately. Up next, lesson twenty-one: a troubleshooting methodology for pulling all of this together.
